title: Frequency Queries
directAnswer: Process insert / delete / 'does any value have frequency exactly x' queries. Keep TWO hash maps in lockstep: valueCount (value → how many times it appears) and freqOfFreq (a frequency → how many distinct values currently have that frequency). Every insert/delete adjusts both maps; the existence query becomes a single O(1) lookup freqOfFreq[x] > 0 instead of scanning all counts.

remember.formula:
insert x: f=valueCount[x]; freqOfFreq[f]--; valueCount[x]=f+1; freqOfFreq[f+1]++
delete x: f=valueCount[x]; if f>0: freqOfFreq[f]--; valueCount[x]=f-1; if f-1>0: freqOfFreq[f-1]++
query x: return 1 if freqOfFreq[x] > 0 else 0
rules: Maintain a second map `freqOfFreq` (count → number of values having that count) so query type 3 is **O(1)**, not an O(n) scan.
On every insert/delete, **decrement the old frequency bucket and increment the new one** — keep both maps perfectly in sync.
On delete, do nothing if the value's count is already 0 — never push a count negative.
Never store a 0 frequency in `freqOfFreq`. A count of 0 means 'no value has this frequency', so don't add a `freqOfFreq[0]` bucket.
Query 3 asks about a **frequency**, not a value: 'is there ANY value occurring exactly x times?'
whenToUse: You need O(1) answers to 'does any element have count exactly x?'
A stream of insert/delete with interleaved frequency questions
Tracking a distribution of counts that changes incrementally
antiSignals: Only ever ask for one specific value's count → a single map suffices, no second map
Need the actual values at a frequency, not just existence → store sets, more memory
Static data, queries only at the end → sort/count once, no incremental maps
Need min/max frequency dynamically → a different structure (e.g. buckets + pointers, as in LFU)
remember.takeaway: When a question targets the *distribution of counts* rather than a single count, maintain a 'frequency of frequencies' map alongside the value map. Keeping the two synchronized turns an O(n) scan into an O(1) lookup — the same idea behind LFU caches and All O`one data structures.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise query type 3 asks about frequencies (not values) and add a second 'frequency of frequencies' map so it's O(1), instead of scanning all counts.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Using only valueCount and scanning its values on every type-3 query (O(n) per query → O(n²) overall), or letting the two maps drift out of sync on delete.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the 'frequency of frequencies' map, keep both maps in sync with a decrement-old/increment-new step, and guard delete so counts never go negative and 0 buckets are never stored.

problemStatement:
Process a sequence of queries, each of one of three types:

- `1 x` — **insert** the value `x` into the data structure.
- `2 x` — **delete** one occurrence of `x` (do nothing if `x` is not present).
- `3 x` — **check** whether any integer currently appears exactly `x` times; output `1` if so, `0` otherwise.

Return the list of answers, one per type-3 query, in order.
constraints: Deleting an absent value is a no-op
Type-3 x is a frequency to test (x ≥ 1 in practice)
understanding: Type-3 queries ask about the *set of current frequencies*, not about any one value. Recomputing that set each time is O(n). Instead, keep a running map from each frequency to how many values currently have it, updated on every insert/delete, so the question becomes one map lookup.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does query type 3 ask about a value or a frequency?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: A frequency: 'is there any value that occurs exactly x times right now?' Misreading this as 'how many times does value x appear' is the classic trap.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What happens when I delete a value that isn't present?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Nothing — it's a no-op. You must guard against decrementing a count below 0.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same value be inserted many times?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the point. valueCount[x] grows with each insert and shrinks with each delete.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Could x in a type-3 query exceed every current count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — then freqOfFreq[x] is 0 (absent), so you output 0. A defaultdict / getOrDefault handles it cleanly.

examples.explanation: First 3-2: no value yet appears twice → 0. By the second 3-2, both 10 (×2) and 6 (×2) appear twice → 1.
First 3-2: value 1 appears once, nothing has freq 2 → 0. After two more inserts and one delete, 1 appears twice → 1.
Initially empty → 0. After inserting 7 once, a value has frequency 1 → 1.

diagrams.caption: Inserts and deletes rewrite both maps; type-3 is a pure read of freqOfFreq.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Single Map, Scan on Query 3
approaches.whenToMention: State it to show the inserts/deletes are easy, then note that scanning all counts per type-3 query is the bottleneck.

complexity.time: O(q × d) where d = distinct values

hints: Inserts and deletes are trivial with one map: valueCount[x] up or down. The cost is hidden in the type-3 query.
For a type-3 query, you need to know whether ANY value has count exactly x. With only valueCount, how do you find out?
You'd scan every entry of valueCount looking for a count equal to x — O(d) per query. With up to 10⁵ queries that's O(q·d), too slow when many are type 3.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Insert/delete are O(1) with one hash map. Each type-3 query scans all d distinct values to test for count == x → O(d). With q queries, the worst case (many type-3) is O(q·d), up to ~10¹⁰.
approaches.explanation:
Keep a single map `valueCount` from value to its current occurrence count. Inserts increment it, deletes decrement it (guarding against going below 0).

**Why the inserts/deletes are fine.** Each is a single hash-map update — O(1) average. Nothing about maintaining individual counts is slow.

**Where it falls apart.** A type-3 query asks 'does *any* value have count exactly x?'. With only `valueCount`, the only way to answer is to walk every entry and check whether its count equals x. That's O(d) per type-3 query, where d is the number of distinct values. If a large fraction of the q queries are type 3, the total balloons to O(q·d) — for q, d near 10⁵ that's ~10¹⁰ operations and times out.

**The redundancy to remove.** Across consecutive type-3 queries the count distribution barely changes — yet we re-scan it from scratch every time. Maintaining a running tally of 'how many values have each frequency' eliminates the rescans, making each type-3 query O(1).
approaches.insight: The slow part is recomputing a global fact (which frequencies are present) on every query when it changes by at most one per insert/delete. Maintaining that fact incrementally — a second map — is the leap to O(1) queries.

dryRun.intro: Single map. Type-3 scans all counts for a match.

java.explanation: Insert: add 1 to x's count, creating the entry if new.
Delete: drop the count by 1, removing the key entirely at 0 so it can't be falsely matched.
Type 3: containsValue scans ALL counts — O(d), the bottleneck.

python.explanation: Delete only if present — never go below 0.

python.line: out.append(1 if x in value_count.values() else 0)
python.explanation: Type 3: 'x in .values()' walks every count — O(d) per query.

diagrams.title: Only valueCount exists; type-3 scans it
diagrams.caption: Answering 'any value with freq x?' means inspecting every value's count.

pitfalls: Using containsValue / x in .values() on every type-3 query — O(d) each, O(q·d) total.
Leaving a value at count 0 in the map — containsValue(0) could falsely match.
Reading type-3 x as a value to look up rather than a frequency to test.

approaches.name: Two Hash Maps — Frequency of Frequencies (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'keep a second map: frequency → how many values have that frequency, so query 3 is O(1)'.
hints: What if you tracked, for each frequency value, how many distinct numbers currently have that frequency? Then 'any value with frequency x?' is a single lookup.
Keep valueCount (value → count) AND freqOfFreq (count → number of values with that count). On insert/delete, move a value between frequency buckets: decrement its old bucket, increment its new one.
Type 3 x: return 1 if freqOfFreq[x] > 0 else 0. Never store a 0-count bucket, and never let valueCount go negative on a delete.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Every query does a constant number of hash-map operations: insert/delete touch valueCount once and freqOfFreq twice; type-3 is one lookup. So O(1) average per query, O(q) total. Space is O(d) for distinct values plus the frequency buckets.
approaches.explanation:
Run two maps in lockstep:

- `valueCount`: value → how many times it currently appears.
- `freqOfFreq`: a frequency → how many distinct values currently have exactly that frequency.

`freqOfFreq` is the 'frequency of frequencies' map, and it's what makes type-3 queries O(1).

**Insert x.** Let `f = valueCount[x]` (0 if absent). The value is leaving frequency bucket `f` and entering `f+1`, so: decrement `freqOfFreq[f]` (only if `f > 0`), set `valueCount[x] = f + 1`, and increment `freqOfFreq[f+1]`. Two bucket edits keep the maps consistent.

**Delete x.** Let `f = valueCount[x]`. If `f == 0`, the value isn't present — **do nothing** (deleting an absent value is a no-op, and decrementing would corrupt the maps). Otherwise the value moves from bucket `f` to `f-1`: decrement `freqOfFreq[f]`, set `valueCount[x] = f - 1`, and increment `freqOfFreq[f-1]` **only if `f-1 > 0`** (a count of 0 means the value is gone — don't track a 0 bucket).

**Query 3 x.** Return `1` if `freqOfFreq[x] > 0`, else `0`. One lookup — no scanning.

**Why the two maps must stay synchronized.** `freqOfFreq` is only correct if it's updated on *every* change to `valueCount`. The discipline is always 'decrement the old frequency bucket, increment the new one' as a value's count changes by exactly one. Skip either half and the maps drift, producing wrong answers later — the subtle bug graders look for.

**Why never store a 0 bucket.** `freqOfFreq[x] > 0` is the existence test. If you ever set `freqOfFreq[0]` to a positive number (e.g. by incrementing `f-1` when `f-1 == 0`), a future query `3 0` would wrongly report 1, and you'd be tracking a meaningless 'values with frequency 0'. Guard the `+1` with `f-1 > 0`.

**Why this is the version to ship.** Every operation is O(1) average, so q queries run in O(q) total — comfortably within limits for 10⁵ queries. The cost is one extra map and the discipline of keeping both in sync.
approaches.insight: The trick is maintaining a derived statistic (the distribution of counts) incrementally instead of recomputing it. Each insert/delete shifts exactly one value between two adjacent frequency buckets, so the update is O(1). This 'second map of frequencies' idea reappears in LFU cache eviction and the All O`one data-structure problem.

dryRun.intro: valueCount = value→count, freqOfFreq = count→#values. Type-3 reads freqOfFreq[x].

java.explanation: Current frequency of x; 0 means it's new.
x is leaving bucket f — decrement it (skip when f==0, no bucket exists).
x now has frequency f+1 — increment that bucket. Maps stay in sync.
On delete, only record the new bucket if f-1 > 0 — never store a 0-frequency bucket.
Type 3 is one O(1) lookup: is any value at frequency x?

python.explanation: x moves out of frequency bucket f (guarded by f > 0).
x enters bucket f+1 — keep freq_of_freq consistent with value_count.
Delete: only register bucket f-1 when it's positive, so freq 0 is never tracked.
O(1) existence check on the frequency map.

diagrams.title: freqOfFreq makes type-3 a single lookup
diagrams.caption: valueCount tracks per-value counts; freqOfFreq tracks how many values sit at each count.

edgeCases.behavior: Delete on empty is a no-op (f==0 → skip). freqOfFreq[1] = 0 → query outputs 0. No negative counts.
Insert 3 (freq 1), delete 3 (freq 0). freqOfFreq[1] decremented back to 0; f-1==0 so no 0-bucket stored → query 1 outputs 0.
9 reaches frequency 3; freqOfFreq[3] = 1 → query outputs 1. Buckets 1 and 2 were vacated along the way.

pitfalls: Updating valueCount but forgetting to update freqOfFreq — the maps drift and queries go wrong.
Incrementing freqOfFreq[f-1] when f-1 == 0 — pollutes the map with a meaningless 0 bucket.
Decrementing valueCount on a delete when the value isn't present — pushes the count negative.

commonMistakes: Scanning all values on every type-3 query instead of maintaining a frequency-of-frequencies map.
Letting the two maps fall out of sync — updating one but not the other on insert/delete.
Reading type-3 x as a value to look up rather than a frequency to test.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Scanning values on every type-3 query
commonMistakesDetailed.why: containsValue / 'x in .values()' is O(d). With many type-3 queries on 10⁵ inputs this becomes O(q·d) and times out. A second map makes it O(1).
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: out.append(1 if x in value_count.values() else 0)  # O(d) scan
commonMistakesDetailed.good: out.append(1 if freq_of_freq.get(x, 0) > 0 else 0)  # O(1) lookup

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Maps drifting out of sync
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you change valueCount without moving the value between freqOfFreq buckets, freqOfFreq no longer reflects reality and later type-3 answers are wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
valueCount.put(x, f + 1);
// forgot to update freqOfFreq

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Storing a frequency-0 bucket
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Incrementing freqOfFreq[f-1] when f-1 is 0 records 'values with frequency 0', which is meaningless and would make a query '3 0' wrongly return 1.

followupVariations.title: LFU Cache
followupVariations.hint: Frequency-of-frequencies taken further: buckets per frequency to evict the least-frequently-used in O(1).

followupVariations.title: All O`one Data Structure
followupVariations.hint: Maintain min/max key frequency in O(1) with a doubly linked list of frequency buckets.

followupVariations.title: Top K Frequent Elements
followupVariations.hint: Bucket values by frequency, then read buckets from the top — bucket sort on counts.

followupVariations.title: Sort Characters By Frequency
followupVariations.hint: Count, then order by count — the static cousin of this streaming problem.

patternNote: Canonical frequency-of-frequencies bookkeeping. When a query targets the distribution of counts (not a single count), maintain a second map (count → #values) in sync with the value map for O(1) answers. Same idea underpins LFU Cache and All O`one Data Structure.
